ecg-cond-001.question: On an ECG recorded at the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s, what duration does one small square (1 mm) represent?
commentaires: Incorrect: 20 ms is the value of one small square at 50 mm/s, a speed sometimes used to analyse P waves or pacing spikes.
Correct: at 25 mm/s, 1 second covers 25 mm, so 1 mm equals 1/25 s, i.e. 40 ms.
Incorrect: 100 ms corresponds to 2.5 small squares; no gridline on the paper equals 100 ms at 25 mm/s.
Incorrect: 200 ms is the duration of one large square (5 mm), not a small one.
ecg-cond-001.explication: At 25 mm/s, 1 second covers 25 mm, so one 1 mm small square equals 1/25 s, i.e. 40 ms. One large square (5 mm) equals 200 ms, and 5 large squares make 1 second. A value of 20 ms would apply at a paper speed of 50 mm/s, which is sometimes used to analyse P waves or pacing spikes more closely. 200 ms is the duration of a large square, not a small one. Routinely checking the paper speed avoids gross errors in interval measurement.
ecg-cond-001.aRetenir: At 25 mm/s: 1 small square = 40 ms, 1 large square = 200 ms.

ecg-cond-002.question: On this regular rhythm recorded at 25 mm/s, measure the RR interval in large squares. What is the heart rate?
commentaires: Incorrect: 50 bpm would correspond to an RR interval of 6 large squares (1200 ms).
Incorrect: 60 bpm would correspond to 5 large squares (1000 ms); misreading by one square is a common error.
Correct: the RR interval measures 4 large squares (800 ms); 300/4 = 75 bpm.
Incorrect: 100 bpm would correspond to 3 large squares (600 ms).
ecg-cond-002.explication: In a regular rhythm, the rate is 300 divided by the number of large squares between two QRS complexes. On this tracing, the RR interval measures 4 large squares (800 ms): 300/4 = 75 bpm. The rule follows from the fact that one minute contains 300 large squares at 25 mm/s. 60 bpm would correspond to 5 large squares, 100 bpm to 3 and 50 bpm to 6. This method only holds if the rhythm is regular; otherwise, count the QRS complexes over a known duration.
ecg-cond-002.aRetenir: HR = 300 / number of large squares between two QRS complexes (regular rhythm, 25 mm/s).

ecg-cond-003.question: At 25 mm/s, the RR interval measures 25 small squares. What is the ventricular rate?
commentaires: Incorrect: 40 bpm would correspond to 37–38 small squares (1500 ms).
Incorrect: 50 bpm would correspond to 30 small squares (1200 ms).
Correct: 1500/25 = 60 bpm; 25 × 40 ms = 1000 ms, i.e. one beat per second.
Incorrect: 75 bpm would correspond to 20 small squares (800 ms), not 25.
ecg-cond-003.explication: The most accurate method in a regular rhythm is 1500 divided by the number of small squares: 1500/25 = 60 bpm. Alternatively, convert to time: 25 × 40 ms = 1000 ms, i.e. one second, hence 60 beats per minute. 75 bpm would correspond to 20 small squares (800 ms) and 50 bpm to 30 small squares (1200 ms). The classic pitfall is mixing up small and large squares in the formula.
ecg-cond-003.aRetenir: HR = 1500 / number of small squares, or 60,000 / RR in ms.

ecg-cond-004.question: In adults, what are the usual limits of a normal PR interval?
commentaires: Incorrect: a PR interval below 120 ms is short and should raise the possibility of pre-excitation or a low atrial rhythm.
Correct: the normal adult PR interval lies between 120 and 200 ms, i.e. 3 to 5 small squares at 25 mm/s.
Incorrect: the upper limit is too generous; a PR interval of 220–250 ms already represents first-degree AV block.
Incorrect: on the contrary, these values define first-degree AV block (PR > 200 ms).
ecg-cond-004.explication: The PR interval is measured from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex and reflects overall atrioventricular conduction (atria, AV node, His bundle and bundle branches). It normally lies between 120 and 200 ms, i.e. 3 to 5 small squares. Above 200 ms, this is first-degree AV block; below 120 ms, pre-excitation or a low atrial rhythm should be considered. The tracing shown has a PR interval of 160 ms, which is therefore normal. Note that a normal PR interval says nothing about the HV interval, which may be prolonged in isolation.
ecg-cond-004.aRetenir: Normal PR: 120–200 ms; > 200 ms = first-degree AV block.

ecg-cond-005.question: In an adult, a QRS duration of 3 small squares (120 ms) at 25 mm/s is compatible with complete bundle branch block.
commentaires: Correct: 3 × 40 ms = 120 ms, the duration threshold for complete bundle branch block in adults, provided the morphology is typical.
Incorrect: the statement is true; 110–119 ms defines incomplete block, and 120 ms meets the criterion for complete block.
ecg-cond-005.explication: 3 small squares × 40 ms = 120 ms. According to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations, a QRS duration ≥ 120 ms in adults is one of the criteria for complete bundle branch block (right or left), together with typical morphology. Between 110 and 119 ms, the terms incomplete block or non-specific intraventricular conduction delay are used, depending on the morphology. Duration alone is not enough: the morphology in V1 and V6 must always be analysed. A broad QRS may also reflect pre-excitation, a ventricular rhythm or hyperkalaemia.
ecg-cond-005.aRetenir: Complete bundle branch block: QRS ≥ 120 ms in adults with typical morphology.

ecg-cond-006.question: The measured QT is 400 ms, with a regular heart rate of 100 bpm. What is the QTc using Bazett's formula?
commentaires: Incorrect: 400 ms is the uncorrected QT; at 100 bpm, it needs correcting.
Incorrect: this value does not match Bazett; Fridericia's formula would give approximately 474 ms.
Incorrect: this is the classic error of dividing by RR (400/0.6) rather than by its square root.
ecg-cond-006.explication: At 100 bpm, the RR interval is 0.6 s. Bazett: QTc = QT / √RR = 400 / √0.6 = 400 / 0.775 ≈ 516 ms. The value of 667 ms results from the common error of dividing by RR instead of its square root. More importantly, Bazett overcorrects at high heart rates: Fridericia (cube root of RR) gives approximately 474 ms. At rates > 90–100 bpm, a linear formula or Fridericia is therefore preferable, or the QT should be measured once the rate slows, before diagnosing a long QT.
ecg-cond-006.aRetenir: Bazett QTc = QT/√RR (in s); it overcorrects during tachycardia, so prefer Fridericia at high heart rates.

ecg-cond-007.question: In adults, what are the limits of the normal frontal-plane QRS axis (AHA/ACC/HRS recommendations)?
commentaires: Incorrect: this range includes marked left axis deviation (left anterior fascicular block) and excludes the normal inferior axis.
Correct: these are the limits of the normal adult frontal axis adopted by the AHA/ACC/HRS.
Incorrect: it excludes the physiological axis between 0° and −30° and includes right axis deviation beyond +90°.
Incorrect: this range is shifted to the right and would include marked right axis deviation.
ecg-cond-007.explication: The normal adult frontal axis lies between −30° and +90°. Beyond −30° is left axis deviation (primarily left anterior fascicular block, but also old inferior infarction, pre-excitation…). Beyond +90° is right axis deviation (left posterior fascicular block, right ventricular overload, slender body habitus). An axis between 0° and −30° remains physiological and is common in elderly or obese individuals. The ranges extending to +120° or +150° would wrongly include marked right axis deviation.

ecg-cond-008.question: The QRS is positive in lead I, negative in aVF and predominantly positive in lead II. What do you conclude about the axis?
commentaires: Correct: a positive lead I, negative aVF and positive lead II place the axis between 0° and −30°, which is still normal.
Incorrect: this would require a negative lead II; the axis would then be beyond −30°.
Incorrect: right axis deviation requires a negative lead I, whereas lead I is positive here.
Incorrect: an indeterminate axis requires both lead I and aVF to be negative.
ecg-cond-008.explication: A positive lead I and negative aVF place the axis between 0° and −90°. To decide, look at lead II (oriented at +60°, perpendicular to −30°): if it is positive, the axis has not gone beyond −30° and lies between 0° and −30°, which remains normal. If lead II is negative, the axis is beyond −30° (between −30° and −90°): left axis deviation, suggestive of left anterior fascicular block. Right axis deviation would require a negative lead I. An indeterminate axis (−90° to ±180°) corresponds to both lead I and aVF being negative.
ecg-cond-008.aRetenir: Lead I+ / aVF−: look at lead II; lead II positive = normal axis, lead II negative = left axis deviation < −30°.

ecg-cond-009.question: According to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations, at what value is the QTc considered prolonged in an adult woman?
commentaires: Incorrect: this threshold is too low and would generate many false positives in women.
Incorrect: an older threshold that is still often quoted, but abandoned because it lacks specificity.
Correct: QTc is prolonged from 460 ms in women (450 ms in men) according to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations.
Incorrect: 500 ms is a threshold for a high risk of torsades, not the upper limit of normal.
ecg-cond-009.explication: The ECG standardisation recommendations define a prolonged QTc as ≥ 450 ms in men and ≥ 460 ms in women. The value of 440 ms, used for many years, generates too many false positives. The 500 ms threshold is not the upper limit of normal but a threshold of markedly increased risk of torsades de pointes, at which QT-prolonging drugs should be stopped. Conversely, the threshold for a short QT is debated at around 360–390 ms. The correction formula used should always be stated.
ecg-cond-009.aRetenir: Prolonged QTc: ≥ 450 ms in men, ≥ 460 ms in women; > 500 ms = high risk.

ecg-cond-010.question: How can you quickly estimate the mean ventricular rate on a 10-second tracing with an irregular rhythm (e.g. AF)?
ecg-cond-010.reponseAttendue: Count the number of QRS complexes over the 10 seconds of the tracing (50 large squares at 25 mm/s) and multiply by 6.
ecg-cond-010.explication: The 300/large squares and 1500/small squares formulas assume a regular rhythm: applied to a single RR interval of an irregular rhythm, they give a misleading value. On a standard 10-second ECG, count the QRS complexes across the whole strip and multiply by 6 to obtain a mean rate per minute. At 25 mm/s, 10 seconds correspond to 250 mm, i.e. 50 large squares. For a more reliable assessment of the ventricular response, Holter monitoring is still needed, since the rate varies with activity.
ecg-cond-010.aRetenir: Irregular rhythm: number of QRS complexes over 10 s × 6.

ecg-cond-011.question: On a standard ECG, the reference calibration is 10 mm per 1 mV and the paper speed is 50 mm/s.
commentaires: Incorrect: the 10 mm/mV gain is right, but the standard paper speed is 25 mm/s, not 50 mm/s.
Correct: 10 mm/mV yes, but 25 mm/s; at 50 mm/s, every interval would look twice as long.
ecg-cond-011.explication: False. The standard amplitude calibration is indeed 10 mm/mV, displayed as a calibration pulse at the start or end of the tracing, but the standard paper speed is 25 mm/s. A speed of 50 mm/s is sometimes used for detailed analysis of P waves or pacing spikes: all durations then look twice as long. The calibration may also be reduced to 5 mm/mV (half standard) when QRS complexes are very large, which distorts the assessment of voltages if it goes unnoticed. Checking these two settings is the first step before any interpretation.
ecg-cond-011.aRetenir: Standard ECG: 10 mm/mV and 25 mm/s — always check the calibration pulse.

ecg-cond-012.question: Regarding QT measurement and correction, which statements are correct?
options: Bazett's formula overcorrects the QT at high heart rates
Fridericia's formula divides the QT by the square root of RR
The QT is measured from P-wave onset to the end of the T wave
A QRS broadened by bundle branch block lengthens the measured QT
In AF, a Bazett QTc calculated from a single RR interval is reliable
commentaires: Correct: Bazett (QT/√RR) excessively lengthens the QTc during tachycardia and shortens it during bradycardia.
Incorrect: Fridericia uses the cube root of RR; the square root is Bazett's.
Incorrect: the QT is measured from QRS onset to the end of the T wave; starting at P-wave onset measures something else.
Correct: QRS widening mechanically lengthens the QT without prolonging repolarisation; use the JT interval instead.
Incorrect: in AF, RR intervals vary; several cycles must be averaged before drawing conclusions.
ecg-cond-012.explication: The QT is measured from QRS onset to the end of the T wave, ideally in the lead where it is longest (often lead II or V2–V3); starting from P-wave onset is wrong. Bazett (QT/√RR) overcorrects during tachycardia and undercorrects during bradycardia, hence the value of Fridericia, which uses the cube root of RR (QT/∛RR) rather than the square root, or of linear formulas. A broad QRS (bundle branch block, ventricular pacing) mechanically lengthens the QT without reflecting prolonged repolarisation: the JT interval can be used instead, or an appropriate correction applied. In AF, variable RR intervals mean several cycles must be averaged; a calculation based on a single RR interval is unreliable.
ecg-cond-012.aRetenir: QT = QRS onset → end of T; beware of Bazett at extreme heart rates, in AF and with a broad QRS.

ecg-cond-013.question: A 28-year-old asymptomatic cyclist has this ECG recorded at a pre-participation sports screening. What is your diagnosis?
options: 2:1 AV block with a blocked P wave hidden in the T wave
Complete AV block with a narrow-QRS escape rhythm
commentaires: Incorrect: no non-conducted P wave is visible between the QRS complexes, and the T waves are all identical.
Incorrect: a junctional rhythm would not have a P wave preceding each QRS with a normal PR interval.
Incorrect: the PR interval is constant; there is no dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes.
Correct: a sinus P wave precedes each QRS with a fixed, normal PR interval at 45 bpm: vagal bradycardia in an athlete.
ecg-cond-013.explication: On this tracing, a sinus P wave (positive in lead II) precedes each narrow QRS with a constant, normal PR interval, at about 45 bpm: the rhythm is sinus and slow (< 50–60 bpm depending on the definition), i.e. sinus bradycardia. In endurance athletes, it reflects physiological high vagal tone. 2:1 AV block would require non-conducted P waves between the QRS complexes, often hidden in the T wave; a junctional rhythm would not have a P wave preceding the QRS with a normal PR interval; complete AV block would show P–QRS dissociation. Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia does not warrant pacing (class III, ESC 2021).
ecg-cond-013.aRetenir: Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia in athletes: physiological, no pacing.

ecg-cond-014.question: A 74-year-old woman presents with presyncope. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Correct: a pause with no P wave whose duration is not a multiple of the PP interval: failure of sinus node automaticity.
Incorrect: the pause (≈ 3.2 s) is not an exact multiple of the baseline PP interval (≈ 860 ms), as type II SA block would require.
Incorrect: no premature P wave deforms the T wave preceding the pause.
Incorrect: AV block requires a P wave not followed by a QRS; here, no P wave appears during the pause.
ecg-cond-014.explication: On this tracing, sinus rhythm (about 70 bpm) is abruptly interrupted by a pause of about 3.2 s with no P waves at all. The absence of P waves during the pause indicates a failure of atrial activity rather than an AV conduction disorder: this is therefore not AV block, which would show a P wave not followed by a QRS. A pause that is not an exact multiple of the PP interval points to sinus arrest (failure of automaticity) rather than type II sinoatrial block, in which the pause equals exactly 2 (or n) PP intervals. A blocked PAC is recognised by a premature P wave, often hidden in the T wave preceding the pause. A symptomatic pause > 3 s warrants discussion of pacing.
ecg-cond-014.aRetenir: Pause with no P wave, not a multiple of PP = sinus arrest; pause of exactly 2 PP = type II SA block.

ecg-cond-015.question: A 68-year-old man reports "skipped beats". Analyse the pause on this tracing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
commentaires: Incorrect: sinus arrest produces a pause with no arithmetical relationship to the PP interval; here it equals exactly two cycles.
Incorrect: Mobitz I would show a non-conducted P wave after PR prolongation; here, there is no P wave during the pause.
Incorrect: respiratory sinus arrhythmia makes the PP interval vary gradually and cyclically, without an abrupt 2-cycle pause.
Correct: the pause equals exactly 2 PP intervals (≈ 1600 ms for a PP of 800 ms): the sinus impulse failed to exit to the atrium.
ecg-cond-015.explication: On this tracing, the baseline PP interval is about 800 ms (75 bpm) and the pause, with no P wave, measures exactly two cycles (1600 ms): the sinus impulse was generated but failed to exit to the atrium. This is type II second-degree sinoatrial block (sinoatrial Mobitz II). Sinus node activity itself is not visible on the surface ECG; the block is inferred from this arithmetical relationship. Sinus arrest would produce a pause that is not a multiple of the PP interval. Mobitz I AV block would show a non-conducted P wave. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia produces gradual, cyclical variations without an abrupt pause.
ecg-cond-015.aRetenir: Type II second-degree SA block: pause equal to an exact multiple of the baseline PP cycle.

ecg-cond-016.question: A Holter recording repeatedly shows progressive shortening of the PP intervals, followed by a pause with no P wave lasting less than two PP intervals. The PR interval is constant. What is the most likely mechanism?
commentaires: Correct: shortening PP intervals followed by a pause < 2 PP: this is Wenckebach at the sinoatrial junction.
Incorrect: type II SA block produces a pause equal to 2 PP, with no preceding shortening of the PP intervals.
Incorrect: sinus arrest does not reproduce this repetitive sequence of shortening PP intervals before the pause.
Incorrect: constant PR and no non-conducted P wave: the block is not atrioventricular.
ecg-cond-016.explication: Type I SA block reproduces Wenckebach periodicity at the sinoatrial junction: sinoatrial conduction time lengthens progressively, with decreasing increments, which shortens successive PP intervals until an impulse is blocked. The pause is then less than 2 PP. The constant PR interval and absence of a non-conducted P wave rule out Mobitz I AV block. Type II SA block would produce a pause equal to 2 PP without preceding shortening. Sinus arrest does not show this repetitive sequence. This is an indirect surface diagnosis with no specific therapeutic implication: correlation with symptoms guides the decision.
ecg-cond-016.aRetenir: Type I SA block: shortening PP intervals then a pause < 2 PP, like Wenckebach at atrial level.

ecg-cond-017.question: Faced with a pause during sinus rhythm, what sign should you look for to suggest a blocked premature atrial contraction rather than a sinus pause?
ecg-cond-017.reponseAttendue: A premature P wave, often hidden in the T wave preceding the pause and deforming it (a T wave that is more peaked, notched or taller than the other T waves).
ecg-cond-017.explication: A very early PAC arrives while the AV node is still refractory: it is not conducted, and it resets the sinus node, hence a pause. Its P wave is often hidden in the preceding T wave, which it deforms (peaked, notched or taller than the others). This is the first benign cause of a "pause" to exclude, by carefully comparing all the T waves. A pause equal to two PP intervals would instead suggest type II SA block, and progressive PR prolongation AV Wenckebach. Blocked PACs in bigeminy can mimic severe sinus bradycardia.
ecg-cond-017.aRetenir: Before calling it a sinus pause, look for a premature P wave hidden in the T wave.

ecg-cond-018.question: A 45-year-old woman reports occasional "ectopic beats". What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Incorrect: a PVC would be broad, with a different morphology and no premature P wave before it.
Incorrect: the abnormal cycles are premature beats; the modest pause that follows is not a sinus pause.
Incorrect: no P wave is blocked; every P wave is followed by a QRS.
Correct: premature beats with an identical narrow QRS, preceded by a P wave whose morphology differs from the sinus P.
ecg-cond-018.explication: On this tracing, a few premature narrow-QRS beats are preceded by a P wave whose morphology differs from the sinus P wave. A premature beat preceded by an abnormal P wave (morphology or axis different from the sinus P wave) with a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS is a premature atrial contraction. The pause that follows is usually non-compensatory, because the PAC resets the sinus node. A PVC would produce a broad QRS without a premature P wave. Mobitz II manifests as a blocked sinus P wave, not a premature beat. A PAC conducted with aberration may, however, have a broad QRS: the premature P wave remains the key.
ecg-cond-018.aRetenir: Premature beat + different P wave + narrow QRS = premature atrial contraction.

ecg-cond-019.question: A 76-year-old woman with known paroxysmal AF has syncope during Holter monitoring: abrupt termination of an AF episode followed by a 5 s pause before the first sinus beat. What is the diagnosis?
commentaires: Correct: a post-conversion pause after an AF episode, the typical form of sick sinus syndrome.
Incorrect: no non-conducted P wave is described; the pause is sinus, not atrioventricular.
Incorrect: there is no prodrome or trigger, and the pause immediately follows termination of the AF episode.
Incorrect: there is no triggering by head rotation or neck pressure.
ecg-cond-019.explication: A post-conversion pause after an AF episode reflects an abnormally long sinus node recovery time: this is the typical form of tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome, a manifestation of sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction). The mechanism is suppression of sinus node automaticity by the tachycardia (overdrive suppression). This is not AV block, since no non-conducted P wave is visible. The context fits neither typical vasovagal syncope (prodrome, trigger) nor carotid sinus hypersensitivity (triggered by head rotation). Here, the documented symptom–rhythm correlation is ideal.
ecg-cond-019.aRetenir: Pause on termination of AF = tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome.

ecg-cond-020.question: In the same patient (tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome with syncope due to a post-conversion pause), which approach is consistent with the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Observation alone, since post-conversion pauses are by nature transient
Implantable defibrillator for prevention of sudden cardiac death
Uptitration of the beta-blocker to prevent AF episodes
Cardiac pacing, or AF ablation in a selected patient
commentaires: Incorrect: syncope due to a documented pause requires action; recurrence is common and may cause injury.
Incorrect: no ventricular arrhythmia is involved; there is no indication for an ICD.
Incorrect: on its own, a rate-slowing drug risks lengthening post-conversion pauses and worsening syncope.
Correct: pacing is class I (ESC 2021); AF ablation (IIa) may avoid it in selected patients.
ecg-cond-020.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in the symptomatic tachycardia–bradycardia form of sinus node dysfunction, to correct the pauses and allow rate-slowing or antiarrhythmic treatment of AF, unless ablation of the tachyarrhythmia is preferred. AF ablation should be considered (class IIa) in selected patients to avoid implantation when the bradycardia is related to AF. Uptitrating the beta-blocker alone could worsen the pauses. An ICD has no role in the absence of ventricular arrhythmia. Observation alone is inappropriate after documented syncope.
ecg-cond-020.aRetenir: Symptomatic tachycardia–bradycardia: pacing (class I) or, in selected patients, AF ablation (IIa).

ecg-cond-021.question: Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia at 40 bpm during sleep warrants permanent pacing.
commentaires: Incorrect: asymptomatic sinus bradycardia, especially at night, is not an indication (class III, ESC 2021).
Correct: pacing is for bradycardia correlated with symptoms, not an isolated nocturnal rate; consider sleep apnoea.
ecg-cond-021.explication: False. Pacing is not recommended (class III, ESC 2021) in asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction or when bradycardia is due to a transient or reversible cause. Nocturnal rates of 35–40 bpm are common, particularly in young people or athletes, owing to vagal predominance. The key decision criterion in sinus node dysfunction is the correlation between symptoms and bradycardia, not an isolated heart rate value. Nocturnal bradycardia should, however, prompt a search for sleep apnoea syndrome.
ecg-cond-021.aRetenir: Sinus node dysfunction: pace bradycardia correlated with symptoms, not a heart rate figure.

ecg-cond-022.question: Before accepting a pacing indication for bradycardia (sinus node dysfunction or AV block), which reversible or extrinsic causes should be sought?
commentaires: Correct: hypothyroidism slows sinus node automaticity and is a classic reversible cause.
Incorrect: hypokalaemia promotes ectopy and tachyarrhythmias; hyperkalaemia is what causes bradycardia and block.
Correct: the most common extrinsic cause, to be reassessed before any implantation (including beta-blocker eye drops).
Correct: sleep apnoea causes nocturnal bradycardia and pauses, often reversible with treatment.
Incorrect: hyperthyroidism causes sinus tachycardia or AF, not bradycardia.
ecg-cond-022.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines stress the search for potentially reversible causes before any implantation: drugs (beta-blockers including eye drops, ivabradine, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, antiarrhythmic drugs), electrolyte disturbances (mainly hyperkalaemia), hypothyroidism, sleep apnoea, hypothermia, acute myocardial infarction and Lyme disease. Hypokalaemia rather promotes ectopic beats, tachyarrhythmias and torsades; it is hyperkalaemia that slows automaticity and conduction. Hyperthyroidism, by contrast, causes sinus tachycardia or AF, not bradycardia. Note, however, that if the rate-slowing drug is essential (e.g. a beta-blocker after myocardial infarction), symptomatic bradycardia may justify pacing without stopping the drug.
ecg-cond-022.aRetenir: Always exclude a reversible cause (drug, K+, thyroid, sleep apnoea, Lyme disease, ischaemia) before pacing.

ecg-cond-023.question: In a patient with suspected sinus node dysfunction who complains of exertional dyspnoea and fatigue, exercise testing is useful to look for chronotropic incompetence.
commentaires: Correct: exercise testing documents chronotropic incompetence, which the resting ECG and Holter monitoring can miss.
Incorrect: the statement is true; exercise allows dyspnoea to be correlated with an inadequate rate and guides rate response.
ecg-cond-023.explication: True. Chronotropic incompetence, i.e. the inability to increase heart rate appropriately during exercise, is a form of sinus node dysfunction that the resting ECG and Holter monitoring can miss. Exercise testing documents it and correlates breathlessness with an inadequate rate. It informs the choice of rate response (R mode) if a device is implanted. The result must be interpreted taking into account rate-slowing drugs and the level of exercise achieved.
ecg-cond-023.aRetenir: Exertional symptoms + suspected sinus node dysfunction: exercise test for chronotropic incompetence.

ecg-cond-024.question: Define tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome and explain why drug management is often difficult without pacing.
ecg-cond-024.reponseAttendue: A form of sinus node dysfunction combining atrial tachyarrhythmias (mainly AF/flutter) and bradycardia (sinus bradycardia, pauses, especially post-conversion pauses). The rate-slowing or antiarrhythmic drugs needed for the tachycardia worsen the bradycardia and pauses: pacing protects against bradycardia and allows these drugs to be used (alternatively: AF ablation in selected patients).
ecg-cond-024.explication: Tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome is a manifestation of sick sinus syndrome: diseased atrial tissue promotes AF and the diseased sinus node recovers poorly after episodes, hence pauses on termination that are sometimes syncopal. The therapeutic dilemma is classic: beta-blockers, digoxin or antiarrhythmic drugs control the tachycardia but worsen the pauses. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) to allow these treatments, unless ablation of the tachyarrhythmia is preferred; AF ablation should be considered (IIa) in selected patients to avoid implantation. Do not forget anticoagulation according to the thromboembolic risk score.
ecg-cond-024.aRetenir: Tachycardia–bradycardia: rate-slowing drugs worsen pauses, hence pacing or AF ablation.

ecg-cond-025.question: A 70-year-old asymptomatic man has this pre-operative ECG. What is the diagnosis?
options: Complete AV block with narrow-QRS escape
commentaires: Correct: constant PR interval of about 280 ms (> 200 ms), with every P wave conducted.
Incorrect: the PR interval measures about 7 small squares (≈ 280 ms), beyond the 200 ms limit.
Incorrect: every P wave is conducted with a fixed PR interval; no P wave is blocked.
Incorrect: the PR interval is constant and each P wave is followed by a QRS: there is no AV dissociation.
ecg-cond-025.explication: On this tracing, every P wave is conducted (1:1 ratio) with a constant PR interval of about 280 ms, above 200 ms: this is first-degree AV block, which is really just conduction delay rather than true "block". In Mobitz I, the PR interval would lengthen progressively until a P wave is blocked. Complete AV block would show dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes. The site is most often nodal, especially with narrow QRS complexes. Isolated and asymptomatic, it does not warrant pacing.
ecg-cond-025.aRetenir: First-degree AV block: PR > 200 ms, constant, every P wave conducted.

ecg-cond-026.question: In first-degree AV block, an isolated P wave may fail to conduct, provided the PR interval of the other beats remains above 200 ms.
commentaires: Incorrect: a single blocked sinus P wave is enough to define second-degree AV block, whatever the PR interval of the other beats.
Correct: first-degree AV block maintains 1:1 conduction; any blocked P wave means second-degree block.
ecg-cond-026.explication: False. First-degree AV block corresponds to prolonged AV conduction time (PR > 200 ms) without any blocked P wave: conduction remains 1:1. As soon as a single P wave is not conducted, this is second-degree AV block (Mobitz I, Mobitz II, 2:1 or high-grade), whatever the PR interval of the other beats. Beware of false blocked P waves: a blocked PAC, which is premature, does not constitute AV block. A very long PR interval (> 300 ms) may, however, cause atrial contraction against a closed mitral valve and symptoms resembling pacemaker syndrome.
ecg-cond-026.aRetenir: First-degree AV block = slowed 1:1 conduction; a single blocked sinus P wave means second-degree block.

ecg-cond-027.question: A 62-year-old woman is being investigated for fatigue. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
options: First-degree AV block with variable PR
commentaires: Incorrect: in Mobitz II, the PR intervals are constant before and after the blocked P wave; here, they lengthen.
Correct: the PR interval lengthens until a P wave is blocked, then shortens after the pause: 4 P waves for 3 QRS complexes.
Incorrect: SA block does not involve a blocked P wave; here, a visible P wave is not followed by a QRS.
Incorrect: a P wave is blocked in every cycle: this is at least second-degree block.
ecg-cond-027.explication: On this tracing, the PR interval lengthens progressively until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts with a shorter PR interval: this is Luciani–Wenckebach periodicity, second-degree Mobitz I AV block. A 4:3 ratio means 4 P waves for 3 conducted QRS complexes. Mobitz II would have a constant PR interval before and after the blocked P wave. Type I SA block has no visible blocked P wave. First-degree AV block has no blocked P wave. With narrow QRS complexes, the site is usually nodal and the prognosis generally good.
ecg-cond-027.aRetenir: Lengthening PR then a blocked P wave = Mobitz I (Wenckebach).

ecg-cond-028.question: A 76-year-old man presents with exertional presyncope. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Incorrect: there is no progressive PR prolongation before the blocked P wave, and no shortening afterwards.
Incorrect: the blocked P wave arrives on time (constant PP interval); it is not premature.
Correct: constant PR intervals before and after a blocked P wave that occurs on time.
Incorrect: three out of four P waves are conducted; it is not every other P wave.
ecg-cond-028.explication: On this tracing, the PR interval is constant and, unexpectedly, a sinus P wave is not followed by a QRS, with an identical PR interval on the next beat. This is the definition of Mobitz II: an unexpected blocked P wave, with constant PR intervals before and after and no preceding prolongation. The blocked P wave arrives on time (constant PP interval), which rules out a blocked PAC, whose P wave would be premature. The site is almost always infranodal (His–Purkinje), often with broad QRS complexes, and the risk of sudden progression to complete AV block is high. This is why the 2021 ESC guidelines give a class I indication for pacing, even in asymptomatic patients, in the absence of a reversible cause.
ecg-cond-028.aRetenir: Mobitz II: constant PR, unexpected blocked P wave, infranodal site, pacing indicated.

ecg-cond-029.question: An 80-year-old woman is referred for a slow pulse. What are the diagnosis and ventricular rate on this tracing?
options: Complete AV block, ventricular rate ≈ 40 bpm
3:2 Mobitz I AV block, ventricular rate ≈ 53 bpm
commentaires: Incorrect: the conducted P waves have a fixed PR interval; there is no AV dissociation.
Incorrect: the PR interval of the conducted beats does not lengthen, and every second P wave is blocked, not every third.
Incorrect: a classic trap; a non-conducted P wave is hidden between two QRS complexes, often in the T wave.
Correct: every other P wave is conducted; ventricular rate = 80/2 = 40 bpm.
ecg-cond-029.explication: On this tracing, every other P wave is not conducted, with an atrial rate of 80 bpm: this is 2:1 AV block, and the ventricular rate is half the atrial rate, i.e. 40 bpm. The trap is to miss the blocked P wave, often hidden in the T wave, and wrongly diagnose sinus bradycardia. In complete AV block, the PR interval would vary (dissociation), whereas here the PR interval of the conducted beats is fixed. 2:1 AV block cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II since two consecutive PR intervals are never seen: its site has to be inferred from other clues.
ecg-cond-029.aRetenir: 2:1 AV block: every other P wave blocked; by definition neither Mobitz I nor Mobitz II.

ecg-cond-030.question: 2:1 AV block with an atrial rate of 90 bpm (tracing below). On the 12-lead ECG, the conducted beats have a constant PR interval of 200 ms and broad QRS complexes with a right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block pattern. What is the most likely site of block?
options: Cannot be determined without an EP study
commentaires: Correct: a normal conducted PR interval and bifascicular block point to disease of the distal conduction system.
Incorrect: nodal block is rather associated with a long conducted PR interval and narrow QRS complexes.
Incorrect: an EP study would confirm the site, but a normal PR and broad QRS make an infranodal site far more likely.
Incorrect: SA block does not produce blocked P waves; here, visible P waves are not conducted.
ecg-cond-030.explication: In 2:1 AV block, a normal conducted PR interval combined with broad QRS complexes (bifascicular block) strongly suggests an infranodal site: the AV node conducts normally and the block lies in the diseased distal conduction system. Conversely, a long conducted PR interval with narrow QRS complexes suggests a nodal site. These are only probabilities (intra-Hisian block can have narrow QRS complexes), but they are not equally likely. An infranodal site carries a poor prognosis and requires pacing. SA block does not involve blocked P waves.
ecg-cond-030.aRetenir: 2:1 AV block: normal PR + broad QRS = infranodal; long PR + narrow QRS = more likely nodal.

ecg-cond-031.question: To localise 2:1 AV block (nodal or infranodal), which statements are correct?
options: Atropine or exercise usually improves conduction in nodal block
Atropine or exercise may worsen infra-Hisian block (to 3:1 or higher) by increasing the atrial rate
Carotid sinus massage worsens nodal block and may paradoxically improve conduction in infra-Hisian block
Wenckebach periodicity appearing on the same recording points to a nodal site
Adenosine improves conduction in nodal block
commentaires: Correct: the AV node is very sensitive to autonomic tone; reduced vagal and increased sympathetic tone facilitate its conduction.
Correct: the His–Purkinje system is rate-dependent; atrial acceleration can worsen infra-Hisian block.
Correct: sinus slowing reduces the rate imposed on the His–Purkinje system and may improve conduction.
Correct: coexisting Wenckebach is a strong argument for a nodal site.
Incorrect: adenosine depresses the AV node and therefore worsens nodal block.
ecg-cond-031.explication: The AV node is very sensitive to the autonomic nervous system: atropine or exercise (reduced vagal tone, increased sympathetic tone) improve nodal conduction, whereas carotid sinus massage worsens it. The His–Purkinje system is little influenced by the autonomic nervous system but is rate-dependent: atrial acceleration (atropine, exercise) can worsen infra-Hisian block, whereas sinus slowing by carotid massage may improve conduction. Seeing Wenckebach sequences alongside 2:1 conduction is a strong argument for a nodal site. Adenosine depresses the AV node and therefore worsens nodal block. When in doubt, an electrophysiological study settles the question.
ecg-cond-031.aRetenir: Nodal block: improved by atropine/exercise, worsened by carotid massage; the reverse for infra-Hisian block.

ecg-cond-032.question: An 82-year-old woman presents with syncope. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
options: 2:1 AV block with bundle branch block
Sinus bradycardia with bundle branch block
commentaires: Incorrect: the PR interval varies from beat to beat; no P wave is conducted with a fixed PR interval.
Incorrect: the P waves, faster than the QRS complexes, do not precede them with a constant PR interval.
Correct: P waves (≈ 80 bpm) and broad QRS complexes (≈ 35 bpm) are completely dissociated.
Incorrect: AIVR is faster (> 40–50 bpm); here, the P waves are faster than the QRS complexes.
ecg-cond-032.explication: On this tracing, the P waves (≈ 80 bpm) and broad QRS complexes (≈ 35 bpm) are completely independent, with variable PR intervals. Complete dissociation between faster P waves and slower QRS complexes indicates third-degree (complete) AV block. The broad QRS complexes at 35 bpm reflect a ventricular (or infra-Hisian) escape rhythm, which is slow and unreliable, exposing the patient to asystole and syncope. In 2:1 AV block, the PR interval of conducted beats would be constant. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is faster (> 40–50 bpm) and typically occurs in the setting of reperfusion. The indication for pacing is class I.
ecg-cond-032.aRetenir: Dissociated P waves and QRS complexes, with P waves faster than QRS = complete AV block.

ecg-cond-033.question: This tracing shows an atrioventricular conduction disorder. Which statements about this type of block are correct?
options: The PR interval lengthens progressively until the blocked P wave
The PR interval is constant before the blocked P wave
The pause containing the blocked P wave lasts more than two PP cycles
The first PR interval after the pause is the shortest of the sequence
The QRS complexes are necessarily broad
commentaires: Correct: this is the definition of the Wenckebach periodicity seen on this tracing.
Incorrect: a constant PR interval before the blocked P wave defines Mobitz II, not Wenckebach.
Incorrect: the pause includes the next PR interval, which is the shortest, so it remains shorter than two PP cycles.
Correct: the AV node recovers during the pause; the next PR interval is the shortest.
Incorrect: the QRS complexes are usually narrow, as the site is most often nodal.
ecg-cond-033.explication: This tracing shows Wenckebach periodicity (5:4 second-degree Mobitz I AV block). The PR interval lengthens progressively until the blocked P wave; the first PR interval after the pause is the shortest, because the AV node has recovered. Because the increment in prolongation decreases from one cycle to the next, the RR intervals classically shorten, and the pause remains shorter than two PP cycles. A constant PR interval before the blocked P wave is, on the contrary, the definition of Mobitz II. The QRS complexes are usually narrow, as the site is most often nodal. Beware of atypical Wenckebach (which is common), in which the increments are irregular: comparing the PR interval before and after the pause remains the most reliable clue.
ecg-cond-033.aRetenir: Wenckebach: lengthening PR, pause < 2 PP, shortest PR after the pause; constant PR before the blocked P wave = Mobitz II.

ecg-cond-034.question: The narrow-QRS conduction disorder seen on this tracing is most often located in the AV node.
commentaires: Correct: narrow-QRS Wenckebach like this is nodal in the vast majority of cases (decremental conduction in the AV node).
Incorrect: the statement is true; an intra- or infra-Hisian site is the exception, especially with a broad QRS.
ecg-cond-034.explication: True. This tracing shows second-degree Mobitz I AV block (3:2 Wenckebach). Narrow-QRS Mobitz I is located in the AV node in the vast majority of cases, a tissue with decremental conduction, which explains the progressive PR prolongation. It is common in young people, athletes and at night (high vagal tone), and its prognosis is generally good. There are exceptions: intra- or infra-Hisian Wenckebach is possible, especially with a broad QRS. When such a site is demonstrated at EP study, the 2021 ESC guidelines consider pacing (IIa) even in the absence of symptoms.
ecg-cond-034.aRetenir: Mobitz I + narrow QRS = nodal in the vast majority of cases.

ecg-cond-035.question: How is high-grade (or "advanced") AV block defined?
options: Complete AV dissociation with a ventricular escape rhythm
≥ 2 consecutive blocked P waves, others conducted
Every other P wave not conducted (2:1 conduction)
PR interval above 300 ms, with 1:1 conduction preserved
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the definition of complete AV block, in which no P wave is conducted.
Correct: 3:1, 4:1… conduction with some P waves still conducted, which distinguishes it from complete AV block.
Incorrect: 2:1 AV block is a separate entity, excluded from high-grade block by definition.
Incorrect: a very long PR interval with 1:1 conduction is still first-degree AV block.
ecg-cond-035.explication: High-grade AV block corresponds to block of at least two consecutive P waves (3:1, 4:1… conduction), while some P waves are still conducted, which distinguishes it from complete AV block. It reflects severe disease, most often infranodal, and shares the class I pacing indication of complete AV block in the 2021 ESC guidelines (in the absence of a reversible cause). 2:1 AV block is excluded by definition. A PR interval > 300 ms is still first-degree AV block, however marked.
ecg-cond-035.aRetenir: High-grade AV block: ≥ 2 consecutive blocked P waves with residual conduction; class I pacing.

ecg-cond-036.question: Overnight Holter: the PR interval appears constant over the 3 beats preceding a blocked P wave, but the PR interval of the first beat after the pause is 40 ms shorter. Narrow QRS. What is your interpretation?
options: Mobitz II AV block, class I pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: in true Mobitz II, the PR after the pause is identical to the PR before it; here, it is 40 ms shorter.
Incorrect: nothing suggests a premature P wave; the blocked P wave occurs on time.
Incorrect: a visible P wave is not conducted; the block is atrioventricular, not sinoatrial.
Correct: the PR shortening after the pause reflects nodal recovery in atypical Wenckebach.
ecg-cond-036.explication: In many atypical Wenckebach sequences, most of the PR prolongation occurs over the first few beats, after which the increments become minimal, creating the illusion of a constant PR interval before the blocked P wave. The most discriminating sign is PR shortening after the pause: it reflects recovery of the AV node and indicates Mobitz I. In true Mobitz II, the PR intervals before and after the blocked P wave are strictly identical. The context (night-time, narrow QRS) also points to vagally mediated nodal block. Confusing the two leads to unnecessary implantations.
ecg-cond-036.aRetenir: Post-pause PR shorter than pre-pause PR = Wenckebach, even if the increments seem to be zero.

ecg-cond-037.question: A patient with syncope has paroxysmal AV block with several consecutive blocked P waves on Holter monitoring. Which finding points to intrinsic paroxysmal AV block (His–Purkinje disease) rather than vagal block?
options: Triggering by an ectopic beat, stable PP, bundle branch block
Sinus slowing concurrent with the block (lengthening PP intervals)
Progressive PR prolongation just before the paroxysmal block
Nocturnal occurrence, during deep sleep, without symptoms
commentaires: Correct: an ectopic trigger, unchanged sinus cycle length and bundle branch block indicate His–Purkinje disease.
Incorrect: simultaneous sinus slowing, on the contrary, indicates a vagal (extrinsic) mechanism.
Incorrect: PR prolongation before the block points to a vagal, nodal origin.
Incorrect: nocturnal occurrence during sleep suggests high vagal tone, not intrinsic disease.
ecg-cond-037.explication: Intrinsic paroxysmal AV block results from disease of the conduction system: it is typically triggered by a premature atrial or ventricular beat (or a change in rate), occurs without any change in sinus cycle length and is often associated with baseline bundle branch block; it requires pacing. Vagally mediated (extrinsic) AV block, by contrast, is accompanied by simultaneous sinus slowing and PR prolongation, and often occurs at night or in a reflex setting. A third entity, idiopathic paroxysmal AV block (associated with low adenosine levels), occurs without bundle branch block or a vagal trigger. Recognising the mechanism avoids implanting devices for vasovagal episodes and missing serious block.
ecg-cond-037.aRetenir: Intrinsic paroxysmal AV block: triggered by an ectopic beat, stable PP, baseline bundle branch block.

ecg-cond-038.question: Acute inferior myocardial infarction. The monitor records the tracing below, which is well tolerated. Which statement is correct?
options: The block is infra-Hisian and warrants immediate permanent pacing
The narrow-QRS escape is ventricular in origin and therefore unreliable
This block has the same prognosis as AV block in anterior infarction
The block is usually nodal, often transient and atropine-responsive
commentaires: Incorrect: a narrow-QRS escape at 50 bpm indicates a high (supra-Hisian) level of block; no upfront permanent pacing.
Incorrect: a narrow-QRS escape arises above the His bifurcation: it is junctional.
Incorrect: AV block in anterior infarction, which is infra-Hisian, has a far worse prognosis.
Correct: nodal block (AV nodal artery, vagal reflex) that often regresses after reperfusion.
ecg-cond-038.explication: This tracing shows dissociation between P waves at 85 bpm and narrow QRS complexes at 50 bpm: complete AV block with a junctional escape rhythm. In inferior infarction, AV block is generally nodal (blood supply to the AV node via the AV nodal artery, most often arising from the right coronary artery, and vagal reflex). The escape rhythm is junctional with narrow QRS complexes, and the block usually regresses after reperfusion: a permanent pacemaker is not implanted upfront. In anterior infarction, AV block reflects extensive necrosis of the septum and the infra-Hisian conduction system, with a broad-QRS escape rhythm and a far worse prognosis. A narrow-QRS escape rhythm is junctional, not ventricular, in origin.
ecg-cond-038.aRetenir: AV block in inferior MI: nodal, narrow QRS, often transient; in anterior MI: infra-Hisian, serious.

ecg-cond-039.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, in a patient who developed high-grade AV block in the acute phase of myocardial infarction, when can a permanent pacing indication be accepted?
options: Within the first few hours, without waiting for reperfusion
If the block persists after at least 5 days of observation
Only after 6 weeks, the time needed for infarct healing
Never: post-infarction block is always reversible
commentaires: Incorrect: pacing upfront leads to unnecessary implantations, as many of these blocks regress after reperfusion.
Correct: ESC 2021, usual indications apply if AV block persists after at least 5 days; temporary pacing in the meantime.
Incorrect: too long a delay, which would require prolonged temporary pacing with its complications.
Incorrect: some blocks persist, particularly in extensive anterior infarction.
ecg-cond-039.explication: AV block complicating myocardial infarction often regresses after reperfusion, especially with inferior infarction. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend applying the usual indications for permanent pacing when AV block has not resolved after a waiting period of at least 5 days after the infarction; in the meantime, temporary pacing is used if needed. Pacing upfront would lead to unnecessary implantations, and routinely waiting six weeks would needlessly prolong temporary pacing and its complications. Conversely, claiming that these blocks are always reversible is wrong, particularly in extensive anterior infarction.
ecg-cond-039.aRetenir: Post-infarction AV block: permanent pacing if it persists after at least 5 days.

ecg-cond-040.question: Complete AV block due to Lyme carditis is often reversible with antibiotic therapy: temporary pacing is initially preferred over permanent implantation.
commentaires: Correct: Lyme carditis is a reversible cause of AV block; temporary pacing while awaiting the effect of antibiotics.
Incorrect: the statement is true; the block usually regresses within days to weeks of antibiotic therapy.
ecg-cond-040.explication: True. Lyme disease is one of the reversible causes of AV block listed in the 2021 ESC guidelines. The block, often nodal and fluctuating, usually regresses within days to weeks with appropriate antibiotic therapy. If pacing is needed, temporary pacing is preferred (possibly using an active-fixation lead connected to an externalised generator) while awaiting recovery. This aetiology should be considered in a young patient with unexplained AV block and a history of tick exposure.
ecg-cond-040.aRetenir: AV block + history of tick bite: think Lyme disease, block reversible with antibiotics.

ecg-cond-041.question: A patient on dialysis presents with fatigue: bradycardia at 38 bpm, broad QRS complexes, tall peaked T waves, no visible P waves. What is the priority?
options: Emergency implantation of a permanent pacemaker
IV atropine followed by monitoring in a high-dependency unit
IV calcium, then treatment of hyperkalaemia (dialysis)
Continuous IV isoprenaline, before any blood tests
commentaires: Incorrect: the cause is reversible; no permanent implantation, and capture is often difficult in hyperkalaemia.
Incorrect: atropine does not correct the mechanism and has little effect on conduction depressed by potassium.
Correct: peaked T waves, broad QRS and absent P waves in a dialysis patient: stabilise the membrane with calcium, then lower potassium.
Incorrect: isoprenaline does not treat the cause; delaying treatment of hyperkalaemia is dangerous.
ecg-cond-041.explication: This picture combines the classic signs of severe hyperkalaemia: tall peaked T waves, flattening then disappearance of P waves, QRS widening and bradycardia (sinoventricular rhythm or AV block). The priority is to stabilise the myocardial membrane with IV calcium salts, then lower serum potassium (insulin–glucose, potassium removal, dialysis). Temporary pacing may be needed, but capture is sometimes difficult in hyperkalaemia. Permanent implantation is not indicated, since the cause is reversible (ESC 2021). Atropine or isoprenaline alone do little to address the mechanism.
ecg-cond-041.aRetenir: Broad-QRS bradycardia with peaked T waves in a dialysis patient: hyperkalaemia until proven otherwise.

ecg-cond-042.question: QRS 130 ms, rSR' pattern in V1, broad slurred S wave in leads I and V6. What is the diagnosis?
commentaires: Correct: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rSR' in V1 and a broad S wave in I/V6 reflect delayed RV activation.
Incorrect: LBBB produces a QS or rS pattern in V1 and broad notched R waves in I and V6.
Incorrect: isolated fascicular block does not widen the QRS to 130 ms or produce rSR' in V1.
Incorrect: there is no short PR interval or delta wave in this description.
ecg-cond-042.explication: Complete RBBB combines a QRS ≥ 120 ms, an rsr', rsR' or rSR' pattern in V1–V2 (R' usually taller than r) and a broad S wave (> 40 ms or longer than the R wave) in leads I and V6. These abnormalities reflect delayed activation of the right ventricle. LBBB, by contrast, produces broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL and V5–V6, with QS or rS in V1. Left anterior fascicular block does not on its own produce a QRS ≥ 120 ms. Pre-excitation combines a short PR interval and a delta wave.
ecg-cond-042.aRetenir: RBBB: rSR' in V1 and broad S in I/V6, QRS ≥ 120 ms.

ecg-cond-043.question: Which criterion is part of the definition of complete left bundle branch block (AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009)?
options: Notched R in V5–V6 with a small septal q wave preserved
Broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6, with no septal q wave
rSR' pattern in V1 with a broad S wave in I and V6
QRS between 100 and 110 ms with a QS pattern in V1
commentaires: Incorrect: a persistent lateral septal q wave should cast doubt on true LBBB.
Correct: reversed septal activation (loss of the lateral q wave) and broad notched R waves in the left-sided leads.
Incorrect: this is the right bundle branch block pattern.
Incorrect: complete LBBB requires a QRS ≥ 120 ms in adults.
ecg-cond-043.explication: In LBBB, septal depolarisation occurs from right to left: the physiological septal q wave disappears in I, V5 and V6, and the R waves are broad, notched or slurred in the lateral leads. V1 shows a QS or rS pattern. QRS duration must be ≥ 120 ms in adults. The rSR' pattern in V1 is that of RBBB. A persistent lateral septal q wave should cast doubt on the diagnosis (non-specific conduction delay, old infarction).
ecg-cond-043.aRetenir: LBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, broad notched lateral R waves, no septal q wave in I/V5/V6.

ecg-cond-044.question: Which criteria are part of the definition of left anterior fascicular block according to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations?
options: rS pattern in II, III and aVF
qR pattern in III and aVF
commentaires: Correct: left axis deviation between −45° and −90°; between −30° and −45°, the criterion is not met.
Correct: qR pattern in aVL, with a delayed R-wave peak time.
Correct: activation starts in the inferoposterior region, hence an rS pattern in the inferior leads.
Incorrect: isolated fascicular block has a QRS < 120 ms; beyond that, a bundle branch block is associated.
Incorrect: qR in III and aVF belongs to left posterior fascicular block.
ecg-cond-044.explication: Left anterior fascicular block is the most common fascicular conduction disorder: activation starts in the inferoposterior region and then spreads upwards and to the left. It combines left axis deviation between −45° and −90°, a qR pattern in aVL (R-wave peak time in aVL ≥ 45 ms), an rS pattern in II, III and aVF, and a QRS < 120 ms: a QRS ≥ 120 ms suggests an associated bundle branch block. The qR pattern in III and aVF belongs to left posterior fascicular block. An axis between −30° and −45° is not sufficient according to the 2009 AHA criteria and warrants a search for another cause.
ecg-cond-044.aRetenir: LAFB: axis −45° to −90°, qR in aVL, rS in the inferior leads, QRS < 120 ms.

ecg-cond-045.question: ECG: axis +120°, rS pattern in I and aVL, qR in III and aVF, QRS 100 ms. Before diagnosing left posterior fascicular block, which diagnosis must be excluded first?
options: Old inferior infarction (q waves in III, aVF)
Acute pericarditis in its early phase
commentaires: Incorrect: inferior infarction tends instead to shift the axis to the left; it is extensive lateral infarction that must be excluded.
Incorrect: the QRS measures 100 ms and nothing suggests peaked T waves; this is not the picture.
Correct: LPFB is a diagnosis of exclusion; right ventricular overload is the first cause of right axis deviation to exclude.
Incorrect: pericarditis alters the ST and PR segments, not the QRS axis.
ecg-cond-045.explication: Left posterior fascicular block is rare, as the posterior fascicle is short, thick and has a dual blood supply. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: other causes of right axis deviation must be ruled out, in particular right ventricular hypertrophy or overload, a slender body habitus, extensive lateral infarction and pulmonary embolism. The AHA criteria combine an axis of +90° to +180°, rS in I and aVL, qR in III and aVF and a QRS < 120 ms. Combined with RBBB, it forms bifascicular block with a poor prognosis. Inferior infarction, by contrast, shifts the axis to the left, and neither hyperkalaemia nor pericarditis produces this picture with a QRS of 100 ms.
ecg-cond-045.aRetenir: LPFB = diagnosis of exclusion: rule out right ventricular overload or a slender body habitus.

ecg-cond-046.question: In an adult, a QRS of 115 ms with an rsR' pattern in V1 and a broad S wave in I and V6 corresponds to complete right bundle branch block.
commentaires: Incorrect: the morphology is that of RBBB, but a QRS of 115 ms defines incomplete block; complete block requires ≥ 120 ms.
Correct: RBBB morphology with a QRS between 110 and 119 ms = incomplete RBBB (AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009).
ecg-cond-046.explication: False. According to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations, an RBBB morphology (rsR' in V1–V2, broad S in I and V6) with a QRS between 110 and 119 ms in an adult defines incomplete RBBB. Complete RBBB requires a QRS ≥ 120 ms. An rSr' pattern with a QRS < 110 ms is often a normal variant, common in young people and athletes. Incomplete RBBB should nevertheless raise the possibility of an atrial septal defect or, with ST elevation in V1–V2, Brugada syndrome.
ecg-cond-046.aRetenir: RBBB: incomplete if QRS 110–119 ms, complete from 120 ms in adults.

ecg-cond-047.question: Which criteria belong to Strauss's strict definition of left bundle branch block, used to predict response to cardiac resynchronisation?
options: QRS ≥ 140 ms in men or ≥ 130 ms in women
QS or rS pattern in V1 and V2
Mid-QRS notching required in all six leads V1, V2, V5, V6, I and aVL
Presence of a septal q wave in V6
commentaires: Correct: a higher duration threshold than the classic definition, differing by sex.
Correct: QS or rS pattern in V1 and V2, reflecting activation moving away from the RV.
Incorrect: mid-QRS notching is required in at least two of these leads, not all six.
Incorrect: a septal q wave in V6 is incompatible with true LBBB.
Incorrect: the axis is not part of the Strauss definition.
ecg-cond-047.explication: Strauss et al. (2011) proposed strict criteria because about a third of "conventional" LBBB actually corresponds to LV hypertrophy combined with non-specific conduction delay. True LBBB requires a QRS ≥ 140 ms (men) or ≥ 130 ms (women), a QS or rS pattern in V1–V2, and mid-QRS notching in at least two of V1, V2, V5, V6, I and aVL: it is not required in all of them. A septal q wave in V6 is incompatible with true LBBB. The axis is not part of the definition. These criteria identify the patients who respond best to CRT.
ecg-cond-047.aRetenir: Strauss LBBB: QRS ≥ 140/130 ms, QS/rS in V1–V2, mid-QRS notching in ≥ 2 leads.

ecg-cond-048.question: With a broad QRS (≥ 120 ms) of supraventricular origin, how can you quickly distinguish RBBB from LBBB by looking at V1?
ecg-cond-048.reponseAttendue: In V1: a predominantly positive QRS with an rsR'/rSR' ("M") pattern = RBBB; a predominantly negative QRS (QS or rS) = LBBB. Confirm in the lateral leads: broad S in I/V6 for RBBB, broad notched R with no q wave in I/V6 for LBBB.
ecg-cond-048.explication: V1 faces the right ventricle. In RBBB, the RV is activated late, producing a positive terminal wave (R') in V1. In LBBB, delayed LV activation moves away from V1, which is therefore negative (QS or rS). The lateral leads confirm: a broad terminal S wave in I and V6 for RBBB, a broad notched R wave with no septal q wave for LBBB. Bear in mind that a broad QRS may also be VT, pre-excitation or a paced rhythm.
ecg-cond-048.aRetenir: Terminal positivity in V1 = RBBB; negative V1 = LBBB.

ecg-cond-049.question: Which combination defines bifascicular block?
options: First-degree AV block + left anterior fascicular block
Incomplete RBBB + associated first-degree AV block
Two consecutive blocked P waves (3:1 AV block)
RBBB combined with left fascicular block
commentaires: Incorrect: first-degree AV block is not a fascicular block; it may be nodal.
Incorrect: neither incomplete RBBB nor a long PR interval defines disease of two fascicles.
Incorrect: two consecutive blocked P waves define high-grade AV block, not fascicular block.
Correct: disease of two of the three fascicles, RBBB + LAFB (common) or RBBB + LPFB (rarer, more serious).
ecg-cond-049.explication: The intraventricular conduction system classically comprises three fascicles: the right bundle branch, the left anterior fascicle and the left posterior fascicle. Bifascicular block involves two of them: RBBB + LAFB (the most common) or RBBB + LPFB (rarer, more serious). Complete LBBB is sometimes considered bifascicular. First-degree AV block is not a fascicular block: it may be nodal. Two consecutive blocked P waves define high-grade AV block.
ecg-cond-049.aRetenir: Bifascicular block = RBBB + LAFB or RBBB + LPFB.

ecg-cond-050.question: The term "trifascicular block" applied to the combination of RBBB + LAFB + first-degree AV block is a misnomer, because the PR prolongation may be nodal in origin.
commentaires: Correct: a long PR interval may result from a prolonged AH (nodal) with a normal HV; only the HV localises the delay.
Incorrect: the statement is true; the true ECG equivalent of trifascicular block is alternating bundle branch block.
ecg-cond-050.explication: True. PR prolongation in bifascicular block may reflect nodal delay (prolonged AH interval) with a normal HV interval, rather than disease of the third fascicle. Only measurement of the HV interval at electrophysiological study can localise the delay. Guidelines therefore prefer to describe the combination (bifascicular block with first-degree AV block). The true ECG equivalent of trifascicular block is alternating bundle branch block, which is a class I indication for pacing.
ecg-cond-050.aRetenir: RBBB + LAFB + long PR is not necessarily trifascicular: only the HV interval localises the delay.

ecg-cond-051.question: A 70-year-old asymptomatic patient is found incidentally to have RBBB + LAFB with a PR interval of 180 ms. According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, what is the pacing indication?
commentaires: Correct: the annual risk of complete AV block is low; follow-up and advice about symptoms are sufficient.
Incorrect: class I applies to Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block and alternating block, not this asymptomatic block.
Incorrect: no class IIa recommendation covers asymptomatic bifascicular block with a normal PR interval.
Incorrect: no heart disease with a high risk of ventricular arrhythmia is described; an ICD has no role.
ecg-cond-051.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines do not recommend pacing (class III) in asymptomatic patients with bundle branch block or bifascicular block. The annual risk of progression to complete AV block is low. Clinical and ECG follow-up is sufficient, with advice to the patient about symptoms that should prompt review (syncope, presyncope). Assessment of LV function is useful, as bundle branch block may reveal underlying heart disease. An ICD has no role in the absence of high-risk heart disease.
ecg-cond-051.aRetenir: Asymptomatic bifascicular block: no pacing (class III).

ecg-cond-052.question: A 72-year-old man has unexplained syncope without prodrome, RBBB + LAFB, LVEF 60%, and a non-diagnostic initial work-up. What is the next step recommended by the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Tilt testing as the first-line investigation
EP study; pacing if HV ≥ 70 ms or infra-Hisian block
Observation, as bifascicular block is not the cause
commentaires: Incorrect: empirical pacing is only a IIb option in elderly, frail patients.
Incorrect: tilt testing assesses reflex syncope, not His–Purkinje conduction.
Correct: pacing (class I) if HV ≥ 70 ms or induced infra-Hisian AV block; if the EP study is negative, an ILR.
Incorrect: syncope with bifascicular block raises concern for paroxysmal AV block; investigation is mandatory.
ecg-cond-052.explication: In a patient with unexplained syncope and bifascicular block, the 2021 ESC guidelines advise considering an EP study (class IIa): an HV interval ≥ 70 ms, or second- or third-degree infra-Hisian AV block during incremental atrial pacing or pharmacological challenge (ajmaline, procainamide…), leads to a class I pacing indication. If the EP study is negative, an implantable loop recorder can document any paroxysmal AV block. Empirical pacing without an EP study is only a class IIb option in elderly, frail patients. Tilt testing does not answer the question of conduction.
ecg-cond-052.aRetenir: Syncope + bifascicular block: EP study, pacing if HV ≥ 70 ms; if negative, an implantable loop recorder.

ecg-cond-053.question: During an electrophysiological study in a patient with syncope and bifascicular block, which result leads to a class I pacing indication (ESC 2021)?
commentaires: Incorrect: a prolonged HV (normal 35–55 ms) but below the 70 ms decision threshold.
Correct: HV ≥ 70 ms in a patient with syncope and bundle branch block = class I pacing.
Incorrect: the AH interval assesses the AV node, depends on autonomic tone and is not part of the decision criterion.
Incorrect: a nodal Wenckebach point at 140 bpm reflects normal nodal conduction.
ecg-cond-053.explication: The HV interval measures conduction time through the His–Purkinje system; its normal value is about 35 to 55 ms. In a patient with syncope and bundle branch block, an HV ≥ 70 ms is considered positive and warrants class I pacing. An HV of 62 ms is prolonged but below the decision threshold. The AH interval assesses the AV node and depends heavily on autonomic tone. A nodal Wenckebach point at 140 bpm is normal. An HV ≥ 100 ms identifies a particularly high risk of complete AV block.
ecg-cond-053.aRetenir: Syncope + bundle branch block: HV ≥ 70 ms at EP study = pacing (class I).

ecg-cond-054.question: Two successive ECGs from the same patient show complete RBBB and then complete LBBB. What is the management according to the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Observation, since the patient is asymptomatic
24-hour Holter, pacing only if complete AV block is documented
Mandatory electrophysiological study before any decision
Pacing indicated (class I), even in the absence of symptoms
commentaires: Incorrect: the risk of sudden complete AV block is high; the absence of symptoms offers no protection.
Incorrect: waiting to document complete AV block exposes the patient to injurious syncope or sudden death.
Incorrect: an EP study is not needed; the ECG pattern is enough to establish the indication.
Correct: alternating bundle branch block is equivalent to trifascicular disease; class I pacing, with or without symptoms.
ecg-cond-054.explication: Alternating bundle branch block (RBBB and LBBB on different tracings, or RBBB alternating with LAFB then LPFB) reflects disease of all three fascicles: it is the ECG equivalent of trifascicular block, with a high risk of sudden complete AV block. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing as class I, with or without symptoms. An EP study is not needed to decide. Waiting to document complete AV block on Holter exposes the patient to injurious syncope or sudden death.
ecg-cond-054.aRetenir: Alternating bundle branch block = class I pacing, even if asymptomatic.

ecg-cond-055.question: An 86-year-old frail woman has recurrent unexplained injurious syncope, bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB) and normal LVEF. An EP study is not feasible. What option do the 2021 ESC guidelines offer?
options: Pacing contraindicated without a prior EP study
commentaires: Correct: in frail elderly patients with injurious syncope, empirical pacing may be considered (IIb).
Incorrect: the 2021 ESC guidelines specifically provide an option without an EP study in these frail patients.
Incorrect: this is not class I; in a patient who can be investigated, an EP study then an ILR remain the rule.
Incorrect: with a normal LVEF, an ICD is not an option.
ecg-cond-055.explication: In elderly, frail patients with unexplained syncope and bifascicular block and a high risk of injurious recurrence, the 2021 ESC guidelines allow empirical pacing to be considered without an EP study (class IIb). This option acknowledges that a large proportion of such syncope is due to paroxysmal AV block, while recognising that the evidence remains indirect. It is not class I: in a patient who can be investigated, an EP study followed by an implantable loop recorder remains the rule. An ICD is only considered if LVEF is reduced.
ecg-cond-055.aRetenir: Frail elderly patient, unexplained syncope + bifascicular block: empirical pacing possible (IIb).

ecg-cond-056.question: A patient has unexplained syncope, left bundle branch block and an LVEF of 30% despite optimal medical therapy. What type of device should be discussed, and why?
ecg-cond-056.reponseAttendue: A defibrillator with resynchronisation (CRT-D) according to the heart failure guidelines, rather than a pacemaker alone: the syncope may be due to a ventricular arrhythmia rather than AV block; LBBB with LVEF ≤ 35% is also an indication for CRT.
ecg-cond-056.explication: In a patient with bundle branch block and LVEF ≤ 35%, unexplained syncope may be due to ventricular tachycardia as much as to paroxysmal AV block. In this situation, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering an ICD or CRT-D according to the guidelines on heart failure and ventricular arrhythmias, rather than a pacemaker alone, which does not protect against sudden cardiac death. LBBB combined with reduced LVEF adds an indication for resynchronisation. An EP study alone is not sufficient to exclude ventricular arrhythmic risk in this setting.
ecg-cond-056.aRetenir: Syncope + bundle branch block + LVEF ≤ 35%: think ICD/CRT-D, not a pacemaker alone.

ecg-cond-057.question: What is the usual rate of a junctional escape rhythm?
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the rate of a ventricular (Purkinje) escape rhythm, with broad QRS complexes.
Correct: the AV junction takes over at 40–60 bpm, with narrow QRS complexes.
Incorrect: this is the rate of sinus rhythm; above 60 bpm, a junctional rhythm is termed accelerated.
Incorrect: a tachycardic rate, unrelated to an escape rhythm.
ecg-cond-057.explication: In the hierarchy of cardiac pacemakers, the sinus node comes first (60–100 bpm), then the AV junction (40–60 bpm), then ventricular or Purkinje cells (20–40 bpm). When the dominant pacemaker fails, the next one takes over: this is an escape rhythm. A narrow-QRS junctional rhythm between 40 and 60 bpm is therefore an escape rhythm; above 60 bpm, it is called an accelerated junctional rhythm. A ventricular escape rhythm is slower, with broad QRS complexes, and less reliable.
ecg-cond-057.aRetenir: Junctional escape: 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS; ventricular escape: 20–40 bpm, broad QRS.

ecg-cond-058.question: A 45-year-old asymptomatic woman has this screening ECG. What is the diagnosis on this tracing, and what can be said about the site of the conduction disorder?
options: Infra-Hisian complete AV block, ventricular escape
Sinus bradycardia, with no AV conduction disorder
Complete AV block, probably nodal, junctional escape
commentaires: Incorrect: a ventricular escape rhythm would be broad and slower (20–40 bpm).
Incorrect: the P waves, faster than the QRS complexes, are not conducted (variable PR).
Incorrect: P waves are clearly present; atrial activity is not blocked.
Correct: P waves (≈ 75 bpm) dissociated from regular narrow QRS complexes (≈ 50 bpm): an escape rhythm arising above the His bifurcation.
ecg-cond-058.explication: On this tracing, the P waves (≈ 75 bpm) are dissociated from regular narrow QRS complexes at ≈ 50 bpm: this is complete AV block (P waves faster than QRS complexes, with no fixed relationship). The narrow-QRS escape rhythm at 50 bpm arises above the His bifurcation: the block is therefore probably nodal (or high in the His bundle). This type of escape rhythm is faster and more stable than a ventricular escape rhythm, hence better tolerated. Sinoatrial block would leave no visible P waves. Congenital AV block, a drug cause or inferior infarction should be considered. Even if well tolerated, persistent complete AV block in an adult warrants pacing (class I, ESC 2021) once a reversible cause has been excluded.
ecg-cond-058.aRetenir: Complete AV block with a narrow-QRS escape at 40–60 bpm = high-level block, junctional escape.

ecg-cond-059.question: In complete AV block, P waves and QRS complexes are dissociated, with the atrial rate higher than the ventricular rate.
commentaires: Correct: no P wave is conducted; the atria beat faster than the ventricular escape rhythm.
Incorrect: the statement is true; if the QRS complexes are faster than the P waves, this is AV dissociation without complete AV block.
ecg-cond-059.explication: True. In third-degree AV block, no P wave is conducted: the atria beat at their own rate (most often sinus) and the ventricles at the slower rate of the escape rhythm. The atrial rate is therefore higher than the ventricular rate. If the reverse is true (QRS complexes faster than P waves), this is AV dissociation due to acceleration of a subsidiary focus or sinus slowing, not complete AV block. The PR interval varies from beat to beat.
ecg-cond-059.aRetenir: Complete AV block: AV dissociation with atrial rate > ventricular rate.

ecg-cond-060.question: Tracing: sinus P waves at 55 bpm, regular narrow QRS complexes at 70 bpm, with no fixed relationship to the P waves; some P waves fall just before or within the QRS complexes. What is the interpretation?
options: Complete AV block with a junctional escape rhythm
AV dissociation due to accelerated junctional rhythm
2:1 AV block with P waves hidden in the QRS
Sinoatrial block with a junctional escape rhythm
commentaires: Incorrect: complete AV block requires P waves faster than the QRS complexes; here, the reverse is true.
Correct: QRS complexes faster than P waves, which fall in the refractory period: interference dissociation, without AV block.
Incorrect: in 2:1 AV block, the P waves would be twice as fast as the QRS complexes, with a fixed conducted PR.
Incorrect: the sinus P waves are visible and regular; atrial activity is not blocked.
ecg-cond-060.explication: Here, the QRS complexes are faster than the P waves: an accelerated junctional focus (70 bpm) takes over from a slower sinus rhythm. The P waves are not conducted because they arrive when the junction is already refractory (P waves within or just before the QRS complexes): this is AV dissociation "by interference", not AV block. Complete AV block requires P waves faster than the QRS complexes, some of which fall at a time when they ought to be conducted. Causes: digoxin toxicity, hypokalaemia, after cardiac surgery, ischaemia, high vagal tone slowing the sinus node. Confusing the two leads to unnecessary implantations.
ecg-cond-060.aRetenir: AV dissociation with QRS faster than P waves = accelerated junctional rhythm, not complete AV block.

ecg-cond-061.question: Describe the hierarchy of cardiac pacemakers and the ECG features of the corresponding escape rhythms.
ecg-cond-061.reponseAttendue: Sinus node 60–100 bpm (sinus P wave, narrow QRS); AV junction 40–60 bpm (narrow QRS, P wave absent, retrograde or dissociated); ventricle/Purkinje 20–40 bpm (broad QRS). The lower the escape focus, the slower, broader and more unstable the rhythm.
ecg-cond-061.explication: Pacemaker cells are organised in a hierarchy: the sinus node, the fastest, normally sets the rhythm and suppresses subsidiary foci (overdrive suppression). If the sinus node fails or block occurs, the AV junction takes over at 40–60 bpm with narrow QRS complexes; P waves are absent, retrograde (negative in the inferior leads) or dissociated. Below this, ventricular or Purkinje foci produce broad QRS complexes at 20–40 bpm, which are unreliable and expose the patient to asystole. This hierarchy helps localise complete AV block from the appearance of the escape rhythm.

ecg-cond-062.question: In the absence of a reversible cause, which situations are a class I indication for pacing according to the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Second-degree Mobitz II AV block in an asymptomatic patient
Permanent complete AV block in an asymptomatic adult
Nocturnal narrow-QRS second-degree Mobitz I AV block in an asymptomatic patient
commentaires: Correct: usually infranodal, with a risk of sudden progression: class I even without symptoms.
Correct: complete AV block with no reversible cause: class I, regardless of symptoms.
Correct: equivalent to trifascicular disease: class I.
Incorrect: asymptomatic bifascicular block is class III.
Incorrect: nocturnal narrow-QRS Mobitz I of vagal origin: no indication in an asymptomatic patient.
ecg-cond-062.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) for second-degree Mobitz II AV block, high-grade AV block or complete AV block, with or without symptoms, once a reversible or transient cause has been excluded. These blocks are usually located below the AV node and carry a risk of unpredictable progression to asystole. Alternating bundle branch block, the equivalent of trifascicular disease, is also a class I indication even without symptoms. Conversely, asymptomatic bifascicular block is class III, and asymptomatic nocturnal narrow-QRS Mobitz I of vagal origin is not an indication.
ecg-cond-062.aRetenir: Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block, alternating block: class I pacing even without symptoms.

ecg-cond-063.question: In an asymptomatic adult in whom the conduction disorder shown on this tracing is permanent and has no reversible cause, pacing is not justified as long as the patient remains asymptomatic.
